data.why: A house with your lamp by its wall, wired to a power plant across the lawn by a pylon and a utility pole; the story follows the power from the plant along the line to the pole, the house, the wall and the outlet. Each problem is seen on the thing itself (heat shimmer on the line, a flash at the lamp, a snapped wire in the storm, smoke out of the wall), each fix lands where the problem was, and it ends close on the lamp lighting up when it is plugged in.

story.title: How electricity gets to your outlet

surprises.claim: Raising the voltage on a transmission line lowers the power lost as heat in the wire.

surprises.claim: A pole transformer steps the street's voltage down to the 120 and 240 volts used in homes.
surprises.search: pole mounted distribution transformer steps down to 120/240 volts homes

surprises.claim: Underground power lines are far less exposed to storm damage than overhead lines.
surprises.search: underground power lines less vulnerable storm damage than overhead

surprises.claim: A circuit breaker trips to cut the power when a circuit is overloaded.
surprises.search: circuit breaker trips overload overheating wire protection

ideas.idea: if you wire a power plant to your lamp, you have electricity
but the long wire turns power into heat
so a transformer raises the voltage to keep it cool
but that voltage would fry your lamp
so a transformer by the pole steps it down
but a storm snaps the wire off the pole
so you dig and bury the cable
but water seeps into the buried cable, and it sparks
so you run the cable inside a sealed pipe
but inside the wall, overloaded wires heat up
so a breaker trips before the wire burns
plug in the lamp, and it lights up
congratulations, you have built the power grid

sentences.text: If you wire a power plant to your lamp, you have electricity.
But the long wire turns power into heat.
So a transformer raises the voltage to keep it cool.
But that voltage would fry your lamp.
So a transformer by the pole steps it down.
But a storm snaps the wire off the pole.
So you dig and bury the cable.
But water seeps into the buried cable, and it sparks.
So you run the cable inside a sealed pipe.
But inside the wall, overloaded wires heat up.
So a breaker trips before the wire burns.
Plug in the lamp, and it lights up.
Congratulations, you have built the power grid.
